---
title: Access
description: How a key or an app is limited to the data and operations it needs, and how each one gets its access.
---

**Each credential reaches only what it was given.** A reading-list app can write bookmarks, read the rest, and see nothing of the owner's tasks.

## Credentials

Two kinds of credential call the API, each sent as `Authorization: Bearer <credential>`:

| Credential | Looks like | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A key | `marfa_k1_…` | What it was made with |
| An app's access token | `marfa_at_…` | What the owner approved for the app |

The owner's browser session is neither. **It counts only on the sign-in and approval pages**: it never reads an item or changes a setting, so a page that rides on the owner's cookie reaches nothing. [What the owner's browser reaches](/run/sign-in-as-the-owner#what-the-owners-browser-reaches) lists those pages.

The server's own machine has one more authority, the [private socket](/run/run-on-a-server#the-private-socket), which the CLI uses to claim an instance, make the first key and recover the owner's password.

## What a credential reaches

A credential is limited in two ways. Its **maps** say which data it reads and writes, and its **permissions** say which other operations it may use.

The reading-list key, made from the CLI:

<Terminal>

```bash
marfa keys create --label "Reading list" --source reading-list \
  --type-permission core.bookmark=write \
  --type-permission 'core.*=read' \
  --type-permission core.task=none \
  --edge-permission about=write
```

```text
marfa_k1_…
key 01a1f14c-0ec4-7088-a16e-77f22ed3958d (Reading list); the plaintext is shown once, keep it now
  core.bookmark   Read and edit
  Built-in types  Read only
  core.task       No access
  edge.about      Read and edit
```

</Terminal>

A map names things at a level, `read` or `write`, and `write` includes reading. Anything a map doesn't name is out of reach. A credential has five maps:

| Map | Field | What it names | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | `type_permissions` | Item types, by ID or pattern | `"core.*": "read"` |
| Edge | `edge_permissions` | [Edge](/build/edges) types | `"about": "write"` |
| Extension | `extension_permissions` | [Extension](/build/properties-and-metadata#extensions) namespaces | `"app.ledger.reminders": "write"` |
| Metadata | `metadata_permissions` | Registering types and edge types | `"types": "write"` |
| Profile | `profile_permissions` | The owner's name, email and avatar | `"email": "read"` |

A few rules apply to single maps:

- **The type map matters most.** Only it takes a third level, `none`, which shuts out a type its wildcard covers. An exact entry wins, then the longest pattern, then `*`.
- **The metadata map** covers the definitions on the instance, not an item's tags and extensions.
- **The extension map** is a key's alone: no app scope names a namespace.
- **The profile map's** `*` at `write` writes the name and avatar. **Changing the email takes `email` named at `write`.**

## What a refusal reveals

An item of a type the credential **can't read** answers `404 item_not_found`, as an item that doesn't exist does, so a refusal reveals nothing. So do its edges, and a blob only such items name. An item the credential can read but not write is refused with `403 type_not_permitted`.

So the reading-list key reads a task as missing, reads a note, and is refused when it changes the note.

<KeyReach />

## Permissions

A permission opens a group of operations, such as making keys. **It opens no items:** a key with every permission and no type map reads nothing, and every item operation is refused `403 type_not_permitted`. The Catalog's [Permissions](/catalog/permissions) page lists all fourteen.

## How an app gets access

**Signing in with OAuth is how an app reaches Marfa.** The instance is its own authorization server: its address is the issuer, the endpoints live under `/oauth`, and `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` lists them. Every app is a public client, holding no secret, and proves itself with PKCE. An AI agent connecting to the [MCP server](/marfa-mcp-server) signs in the same way.

1. The app registers itself and names the scopes it wants. One that names none asks to read and write every type outside `system` and `marfa`, and the edges between items, with `offline_access`.
2. It sends the owner to the approval page, where the owner chooses **Full access**, or **Choose access** to give it less.
3. The app exchanges the code for an access token and a refresh token.

The app then holds a **grant**, exactly what the owner approved, and writes under the source `oauth:<client_id>`. A grant outlives the browser session that approved it. The owner can narrow it, and it lasts until the owner disconnects the app or the app goes unused for `grant_inactivity_days`, a year by default.

A web page connects the same way. Once the owner approves it, its address may call the instance from a browser, and `cors_origins` adds others. No answer allows credentials, so a page reaches only what its token holds.

[Authenticate](/build/authenticate) and [Connect a web page](/build/connect-a-web-page) show the app's side, and [Manage apps](/run/manage-apps#narrow-or-disconnect-an-app) the owner's.

## How a key gets access

A key suits a script, your own agent or a [connector](/build/connectors). The owner makes one from the CLI, and any key or app holding `keys.mint` can make another. A made key holds only the maps and permissions its maker holds, and its expiry is never later than its maker's. A key an app makes stays within the app's grant, can name no extension namespace, and carries the app's `oauth_client_id`. [Manage keys](/run/manage-keys) shows how.

The rules behind this page are in the [keys and sign-in](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/keys-and-oauth.md) and [authentication](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/authentication.md#where-a-browser-session-counts) chapters of the contract.
